extracted.intended_audience: Federal agencies preparing NEPA documents (EISs) and public commenters/NEPA practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for preparing Environmental Impact Statements (EISs) under NEPA, including what effects to analyze (climate, environmental justice), expectations for scientific methodology, handling of incomplete information, scoping summaries, and standards for public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'Federal resources'
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ adds the word 'Federal' to §1502.16(a)(4) consistent with the statute and interprets the phrase 'Federal resources' to mean resources owned by the Federal Government or held in trust for Tribal Nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declines to expand the phrase to include resources committed by other entities; the insertion follows statutory text (42 U.S.C. 4332(2)(C)(v)). This is a definitional clarification for what agencies should analyze under 'Federal resources.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of governmental plans, policies, and controls (including climate plans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must analyze possible conflicts between the proposed action and the objectives of Federal, regional, State, Tribal and local plans, policies, and controls for the area concerned; the final rule broadens 'land use plans' to 'plans' and explicitly includes plans addressing climate change as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to climate change plans is an example (consistent with 2023 GHG guidance) and does not require agencies to resolve conflicts—only to discuss possible conflicts. CEQ retains 'policies' to include formally adopted positions of government entities. CEQ will not modify this provision to address specific project types (e.g., multi-State) but may provide future guidance if confusion arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required analysis of reasonably foreseeable climate change-related effects
rubrics_metrics.description: EIS discussions must include any reasonably foreseeable climate change-related effects, including effects of climate change on the proposed action and alternatives (which may in turn alter the effects of the proposed action and alternatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ incorporates the reasonable-foreseeability limitation (NEPA §102(2)(C)(i)) and the definition of 'effects' to encompass reasonably foreseeable indirect and cumulative effects. CEQ adds the qualifier 'where applicable' to acknowledge not all actions will have climate-related effects that require analysis. The rule is consistent with relevant case law requiring consideration of reasonably foreseeable climate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address risk reduction, resiliency, and adaptation measures in proposed actions and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must address any risk reduction, resiliency, or adaptation measures included in the proposed action and alternatives in the EIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ notes agencies may incorporate programmatic or prior planning analyses by reference and may discuss measures generally if final design occurs after NEPA. Agencies have experience analyzing actions before final design and can similarly analyze resiliency/adaptation measures. CEQ added this to ensure consideration of resiliency to risks associated with a changing climate (wildfires, extreme heat, drought, flood risk, loss of cultural resources, food scarcity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where feasible, quantify greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions for proposed action and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adds the phrase 'where feasible, quantification of greenhouse gas emissions from the proposed action and alternatives' to §1502.16(a)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This incorporates CEQ's 2023 GHG guidance recommendations and aligns with case law (e.g., Food & Water Watch v. FERC; Sierra Club v. FERC) that agencies should quantify and consider downstream carbon emissions or explain why they cannot. CEQ acknowledges flexibility where quantification is not feasible and uses 'where applicable'/'where feasible' qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate analyses must be limited to effects that meet NEPA's causation and foreseeability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must analyze climate-related effects that meet the definition of 'effects'—i.e., are reasonably foreseeable and have the requisite causal relationship to the proposed action; the rule does not require agencies to go beyond what case law already requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ rejects the view that the rule rewrites causation standards; it requires analysis of climate-related effects that are reasonably foreseeable. The final text includes qualifiers to avoid requiring discussion of remote or speculative effects. Agencies should apply the rule of reason and case-law limits on causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of effects in §1502.16(a) is illustrative, not exhaustive; agencies determine relevance case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of effects in §1502.16(a) (including climate change and environmental justice effects) is not exhaustive; agencies must determine on a case-by-case basis which effects are relevant to address in an EIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ emphasizes that recognizing climate change and environmental justice effects does not elevate them above other resource concerns; agencies retain discretion to identify relevant effects for each EIS. The final rule adds qualifiers such as 'where applicable' to reflect that not all items on the list will apply to every action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental justice analysis where applicable (disproportionate and adverse effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must discuss 'where applicable' disproportionate and adverse human health and environmental effects on communities with environmental justice concerns in EISs (finalized in §1502.16(a)(13)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ modified proposed text to replace 'The potential for' with 'Where applicable' and omitted 'potential' because the final rule requires that listed effects be reasonably foreseeable. CEQ will not require agencies to address speculative or non-reasonably-foreseeable EJ effects; agencies should determine applicability case-by-case. Some commenters requested more detailed guidance; CEQ may provide guidance in the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and social effects wording change (no elevated priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ strikes the phrase 'and give appropriate consideration to' from §1502.16(b) to avoid language that could be read to require decisionmakers to give economic or social effects higher priority than other effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declines to add more specificity (e.g., mandatory housing analyses) because such specific requirements are unnecessary in the regulations and housing-related effects are a subset of social and economic effects. Historic and cultural resources remain addressed elsewhere (§1502.16(a)(10) and (a)(5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of scoping information required in draft EISs (§1502.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must include a summary of the information they receive from commenters during the scoping process in draft EISs (retitled 'Summary of scoping information').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ allows flexibility in where the summary is placed (in the draft EIS or an appendix or scoping report). The summary should include information submitted during scoping, including alternatives and analyses, but the provision does not require a summary of every individual alternative, piece of information, or analysis. CEQ rejects the view that preparing a summary is a significant burden because a lengthy, detailed summary is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative public availability of scoping comments (not via FOIA-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies can append comments received during scoping to the draft EIS or otherwise make them publicly available; CEQ did not change 'publish' to language that could be read to allow availability only via FOIA requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent is affirmative public disclosure (e.g., appendix, scoping report), not reactive FOIA-only disclosure. CEQ added conforming edits to ensure agencies have flexibility in meeting the requirement through common practices like scoping reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deletion of redundant 'invite comment on submitted alternatives' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ deletes 40 CFR 1502.17(a)(2) and (b) (2020) and removes the 2020-rule requirement in §1503.1(a)(3) that agencies invite comment specifically on submitted alternatives, as redundant with part 1503 requirements inviting comment on draft EISs in their entirety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ concludes inviting comment on all sections of draft EISs makes the specific invitation unnecessary and redundant; the change reduces regulatory duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to obtain incomplete information when essential and reasonable (§1502.21(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must obtain information relevant to reasonably foreseeable significant adverse effects when that information is essential to a reasoned choice between alternatives, the overall costs of obtaining it are not unreasonable, and the means of obtaining that information are known (CEQ removes 'but available').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ re-adopts its longstanding interpretation (from 1986) that 'incomplete information' refers to new scientific/technical research that is only unobtainable because costs are exorbitant; 'unavailable information' is when means to obtain are not known. Agencies should explain their rationale when they determine it is unreasonable or unnecessary to obtain new information and should identify incomplete information early. If information can be obtained within reasonable costs but not within statutory timeframes, agencies may set new deadlines that allow only as much time as necessary, so long as costs (including delay costs) are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and limits for 'incomplete' vs 'unavailable' information
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ clarifies that 'incomplete information' refers to new scientific or technical research (costs unreasonable), while 'unavailable information' refers to information that cannot be obtained because the means to obtain it are not known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restores CEQ's 1986 interpretation and rejects the 2020 interpretation that treated new research as 'unavailable.' This reading is consistent with NEPA amendments (section 106(b)(3)) limiting when new scientific research is required. Agencies should rely on these distinctions when deciding whether to undertake new research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove 'adverse' modifier from 'significant adverse effects' (terminology alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ removes the modifier 'adverse' from 'significant adverse effects' throughout the section because the final rule defines 'significant effects' to be adverse effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a clarity and consistency edit aligning terminology with the final rule's definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology and scientific accuracy; ensure professional and scientific integrity across NEPA documents (§1506.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must ensure the professional integrity, including scientific integrity, of discussions and analyses in NEPA documents, promote use of high-quality information, explain assumptions, and where appropriate incorporate projections (including climate projections) in evaluations of reasonably foreseeable effects. CEQ moves this provision from part 1502 (§1502.23) to part 1506 (§1506.6) to clarify applicability to all NEPA documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ received confusion about applicability; moving to part 1506 makes clear the obligation applies to all NEPA documents, not just EISs. For detailed guidance on specific changes and final text, CEQ references section II.H.4 of the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment specificity standard (§1503.3): 'as specific as possible' and lower barriers to participation
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ finalizes edits to §1503.3 clarifying that comments should be 'as specific as possible' but removes the 2020-rule language requiring comments to be 'as detailed as necessary to meaningfully participate and fully inform the agency of the commenter's position.' Commenters do not need to describe their data, sources, or methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ found the 2020 language ambiguous and potentially exclusionary, possibly requiring commenters to be technical experts or hire consultants. Removing that language reduces barriers to public participation. Agencies should not interpret the rule to require personal moral explanations or unrelated detailed positions; commenters lacking technical expertise can still meaningfully participate.
